items.title: The Cyber Risk Discourse is Broken
items.summary: I’ve had one too many discussions on the cyber risks of open models — where someone assumes that either banning open models happens in a silo (and bad actors will somehow actually be stopped) or that China is a threat and doesn’t care about AI safety — that I feel we’re going to end up making policy decisions that both limit American AI competitiveness and increases long-term cyber risk. I feel like we’re locked in on a path of lose-lose situation, unless people embrace nuance, trade-offs, and scary realities. Much has been written about the views of various players in this debate, which I summarize as follows: Open weight models pose an untenable risk to society’s functionality , occupied by frontier lab leadership and the national security community in the U.S. Western voices saying open weight models are necessary for defense and banning them will make the world less safe , occupied by AI risk moderates to different extremes. I include myself in this bucket, along with Hugging Face’s perspective after the OpenAI incident, and others like Joshua Saxe . Chinese companies continuing to release open-weight models with strong cyber capabilities , who are making decisions based on the risk assessments of their society and government. This list is also organized by volume or clarity of message in the Western AI ecosystem. The risk-focused discussions have been disproportionately visible, including pieces of work which I view as very detrimental to potential of engaging across assumed party lines on this issue. There’s also very little substantive engagement trying to understand how Chinese companies assess risk — rather, mostly arguments that border on ad hominem attacks like “Chinese labs don’t care about safety.” Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber. The delusions of the anti open-weight alliance The most recent publication from the “open-weights are dangerous” crowd was the report by Anthropic on the risks of GLM-5.3 as an offensive cyber tool. The problem with this is not the technical research they did, which is largely reasonable, but the failure to engage on more cross cutting questions like: What happens if we ban open models due to cyber risks or why do Chinese companies deem these models safe to release? These questions, which I’ll come back to, are the ones we need to answer to understand the ecosystem perspective on current AI risks. All policy actions happen in a multi-piece puzzle, where the shape of risk can be changed, but it is rare that you get a universally better outcome. They are all trade-offs. This sort of solipsistic writing by Anthropic fits very closely to another type of discourse I’m hearing about regularly that is determining the fate of open models and AI broadly — classified briefings. I’ve had many discussions with people who say something like “Look, I’m pro open models, but if you’re seeing what I’m seeing, it’s an onslaught out there due to [XYZ Chinese open-weight model] and we need to act.” This perspective flies in the face of public information, where to date closed models have been documented as the cause of most existing cyber attacks. As someone who tries to make grounded predictions, the evidence of numerous attacks from OpenAI models is the only data I have on the shape of cyber risks (or, you can broaden the scope to include all of FelonyBench ). There are a few possible explanations, and it’ll take years to get to the true answer: Maybe open model weights and closed model APIs (with some safe guards) are both far closer to being easy to mis-use, rather than API models being closer to safe. The trope "Open Dangerous, Closed Safe" may be closer to "Open Unsafe, Closed Unsafe." Maybe there are far fewer bad actors who are willing to use AI models for “loud” cyber attacks that target crucial infrastructure in the US or powerful and underprepared institutions. Closed models have stronger capabilities and stronger safeguards (in theory), but the stronger capabilities part could matter more in net harm if the safeguards on both are porous. I have a lot more to learn about how the cybersecurity ecosystem works, so I won’t support this full-heartedly as one of my current recommendations, but I think it’s at least a reasonable argument that open weight models as a diffusion tool for cyber defense could be the best tool we have to prevent harm over the next few years. There are many domains, e.g. sensitive government agencies, where open-weight models are the only tools that can be deployed in the near-term on air-gapped networks. Lots of this situation seems like the messy reality being hard to pin down, where the logical limits are clearer. I may agree with the simple reality that closed models are far safer in the limit, as a technical tool with more layers of protection, but they may actually be causing more harm in the near term because of how accessible model APIs are. Still, much of the impact of the tools comes down to how they’re used and controlled. A duopoly on such a crucial tool may be the defining, risky part. This is the debate we’re having, and over time, as intelligence diffuses, many things may change. These together make me come to the conclusion that if you think the latest open-weight models need to be banned to slow the diffusion of cyber risks, you probably also need to make public-facing APIs for the frontier closed-models illegal. The current stack of safeguards on closed models is stronger than open-weight models, but far from perfect. It is very likely that cyber capabilities of closed models increase much faster than guardrail performance, and a world where open models are banned while closed models continue to progress would be increasing the offense-defense cyber gap. It will take meaningful time to build mitigations that allow defenders to use strong AI models on their private infrastructure if we remove access to strong open-weight models. Share Explaining China’s AI risk posture China cares about AI safety. They have come to this discourse in a complete, endogenous manner relating to Chinese culture and power structures. There are some big picture pieces of this puzzle that reflect in other ways, such as Chinese society’s techno-optimism that extends into AI and the Chinese government’s complete focus on political stability. These things do, of course, interface with emerging AI risks like cybersecurity. They are in their own AI risk dynamic, which hasn’t risen to the prominence of the political dance between the White House and the frontier labs which we have followed in the U.S. for a few months. My understanding is that the Chinese companies have to register every major model release with the Chinese government. This includes evaluations, which originated around information control for banned government information. It is unclear if this framework has expanded meaningfully into any risks like cyber or bio. The Chinese government is very decentralized and information from the labs needs to go through existing structures to make it to the top. At the same time, there is a much stronger air of social risk in China, where leading AI researchers aren’t allowed to leave the country and the industry is closing off to foreign investment. On balance I would guess the personal risks facing people by unleashing any domestic harms would be much higher than in the U.S., where the worst case is that your company gets deleted. Overall, the political oversight seems much earlier than in the U.S. The Western AI companies’ core principle is close to “the best way to stop a bad guy with AI is to be a good guy with AI.” In China, these companies are much more practical about building a wonderful tool, and in many cases building a tool that complements their existing businesses. I do think that the companies consider the global implications of their work. These labs also clearly are incentivized, and often pushed via the government (at least in public messaging) to compete as much as they can. Running comprehensive safety evaluations on a frontier model like Kimi K3 could cost tens of millions of dollars in compute. These labs would much rather leave that for training. The correct debate is “what is the correct minimum amount of compute a lab should spend on safety testing before releasing each model?” There’s surely a case to be made that it’s more than the Chinese labs do, or at least they should be more transparent on what they do, but I would be hard pressed to agree if you said the minimum amount of compute would match what Anthropic or OpenAI does. It is not clear that, for all the effort Anthropic and OpenAI make on creating an institution that prioritizes understanding risks, they put it before business value and economic success in their priority stack. This “hands off the wheel” vibe from incidents like the HuggingFace—OpenAI incident was one of my lasting takeaways . It’s exemplified in the Hacktron hacking of OpenAI — it’s hard to be the world’s trust cyber partner if your own house is teeming with leaks. I trust many of the individuals at the labs to work hard to ensure safety, but I’m not trustworthy of the institutions overall. Open-weight Mythos in April would’ve been fine? When Claude Mythos was announced, it was previewed as if it was a new class of cyber weapon, where if it ended up in the wrong hands it would’ve caused mass societal destabilization. It seems like this was wrong. By all measures, GLM-5.3 is the model that crosses that threshold of capability, and there’s little public evidence that much has changed, and we’re over a month out of the model weight release. In fact, I would go further. If Claude Mythos was accidentally released as open-weight, it seems like the world would have been more or less fine. Yes, there would be a clear increase in cybersecurity incidents and it would be bad for society if the model leaked, but it would be a scenario that looks more like an acceleration than a step change in risk. The leading proponents of this new wave of open-weight fear mongering have effectively been making a falsifiable prediction — that the current open-weight models are going to cause substantial, not seen before AI harms by crippling our cyber infrastructure. Based on all the evidence I have, which I’ve unpacked above, they’re set up to be wrong. At least now, after so many years of debating open weight risks, we will start to get some real answers. Thanks to Rohit Krishnan and Joshua Saxe for some feedback on this post.
items.summary_html:
I’ve had one too many discussions on the cyber risks of open models — where someone assumes that either banning open models happens in a silo (and bad actors will somehow actually be stopped) or that China is a threat and doesn’t care about AI safety — that I feel we’re going to end up making policy decisions that both limit American AI competitiveness and increases long-term cyber risk. I feel like we’re locked in on a path of lose-lose situation, unless people embrace nuance, trade-offs, and scary realities.

Much has been written about the views of various players in this debate, which I summarize as follows:

  1. Open weight models pose an untenable risk to society’s functionality, occupied by frontier lab leadership and the national security community in the U.S.

  2. Western voices saying open weight models are necessary for defense and banning them will make the world less safe, occupied by AI risk moderates to different extremes. I include myself in this bucket, along with Hugging Face’s perspective after the OpenAI incident, and others like Joshua Saxe.

  3. Chinese companies continuing to release open-weight models with strong cyber capabilities, who are making decisions based on the risk assessments of their society and government.

This list is also organized by volume or clarity of message in the Western AI ecosystem. The risk-focused discussions have been disproportionately visible, including pieces of work which I view as very detrimental to potential of engaging across assumed party lines on this issue. There’s also very little substantive engagement trying to understand how Chinese companies assess risk — rather, mostly arguments that border on ad hominem attacks like “Chinese labs don’t care about safety.”

Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber.

The delusions of the anti open-weight alliance

The most recent publication from the “open-weights are dangerous” crowd was the report by Anthropic on the risks of GLM-5.3 as an offensive cyber tool. The problem with this is not the technical research they did, which is largely reasonable, but the failure to engage on more cross cutting questions like: What happens if we ban open models due to cyber risks or why do Chinese companies deem these models safe to release?

These questions, which I’ll come back to, are the ones we need to answer to understand the ecosystem perspective on current AI risks. All policy actions happen in a multi-piece puzzle, where the shape of risk can be changed, but it is rare that you get a universally better outcome. They are all trade-offs.

This sort of solipsistic writing by Anthropic fits very closely to another type of discourse I’m hearing about regularly that is determining the fate of open models and AI broadly — classified briefings. I’ve had many discussions with people who say something like “Look, I’m pro open models, but if you’re seeing what I’m seeing, it’s an onslaught out there due to [XYZ Chinese open-weight model] and we need to act.”

This perspective flies in the face of public information, where to date closed models have been documented as the cause of most existing cyber attacks. As someone who tries to make grounded predictions, the evidence of numerous attacks from OpenAI models is the only data I have on the shape of cyber risks (or, you can broaden the scope to include all of FelonyBench). There are a few possible explanations, and it’ll take years to get to the true answer:

  • Maybe open model weights and closed model APIs (with some safe guards) are both far closer to being easy to mis-use, rather than API models being closer to safe. The trope "Open Dangerous, Closed Safe" may be closer to "Open Unsafe, Closed Unsafe."

  • Maybe there are far fewer bad actors who are willing to use AI models for “loud” cyber attacks that target crucial infrastructure in the US or powerful and underprepared institutions. Closed models have stronger capabilities and stronger safeguards (in theory), but the stronger capabilities part could matter more in net harm if the safeguards on both are porous.

  • I have a lot more to learn about how the cybersecurity ecosystem works, so I won’t support this full-heartedly as one of my current recommendations, but I think it’s at least a reasonable argument that open weight models as a diffusion tool for cyber defense could be the best tool we have to prevent harm over the next few years. There are many domains, e.g. sensitive government agencies, where open-weight models are the only tools that can be deployed in the near-term on air-gapped networks.

Lots of this situation seems like the messy reality being hard to pin down, where the logical limits are clearer. I may agree with the simple reality that closed models are far safer in the limit, as a technical tool with more layers of protection, but they may actually be causing more harm in the near term because of how accessible model APIs are. Still, much of the impact of the tools comes down to how they’re used and controlled. A duopoly on such a crucial tool may be the defining, risky part. This is the debate we’re having, and over time, as intelligence diffuses, many things may change.

These together make me come to the conclusion that if you think the latest open-weight models need to be banned to slow the diffusion of cyber risks, you probably also need to make public-facing APIs for the frontier closed-models illegal. The current stack of safeguards on closed models is stronger than open-weight models, but far from perfect. It is very likely that cyber capabilities of closed models increase much faster than guardrail performance, and a world where open models are banned while closed models continue to progress would be increasing the offense-defense cyber gap. It will take meaningful time to build mitigations that allow defenders to use strong AI models on their private infrastructure if we remove access to strong open-weight models.

Share

Explaining China’s AI risk posture

China cares about AI safety. They have come to this discourse in a complete, endogenous manner relating to Chinese culture and power structures. There are some big picture pieces of this puzzle that reflect in other ways, such as Chinese society’s techno-optimism that extends into AI and the Chinese government’s complete focus on political stability. These things do, of course, interface with emerging AI risks like cybersecurity.

They are in their own AI risk dynamic, which hasn’t risen to the prominence of the political dance between the White House and the frontier labs which we have followed in the U.S. for a few months. My understanding is that the Chinese companies have to register every major model release with the Chinese government. This includes evaluations, which originated around information control for banned government information. It is unclear if this framework has expanded meaningfully into any risks like cyber or bio. The Chinese government is very decentralized and information from the labs needs to go through existing structures to make it to the top.

At the same time, there is a much stronger air of social risk in China, where leading AI researchers aren’t allowed to leave the country and the industry is closing off to foreign investment. On balance I would guess the personal risks facing people by unleashing any domestic harms would be much higher than in the U.S., where the worst case is that your company gets deleted.

Overall, the political oversight seems much earlier than in the U.S. The Western AI companies’ core principle is close to “the best way to stop a bad guy with AI is to be a good guy with AI.” In China, these companies are much more practical about building a wonderful tool, and in many cases building a tool that complements their existing businesses.

I do think that the companies consider the global implications of their work. These labs also clearly are incentivized, and often pushed via the government (at least in public messaging) to compete as much as they can. Running comprehensive safety evaluations on a frontier model like Kimi K3 could cost tens of millions of dollars in compute. These labs would much rather leave that for training.

The correct debate is “what is the correct minimum amount of compute a lab should spend on safety testing before releasing each model?” There’s surely a case to be made that it’s more than the Chinese labs do, or at least they should be more transparent on what they do, but I would be hard pressed to agree if you said the minimum amount of compute would match what Anthropic or OpenAI does. It is not clear that, for all the effort Anthropic and OpenAI make on creating an institution that prioritizes understanding risks, they put it before business value and economic success in their priority stack. This “hands off the wheel” vibe from incidents like the HuggingFace—OpenAI incident was one of my lasting takeaways. It’s exemplified in the Hacktron hacking of OpenAI — it’s hard to be the world’s trust cyber partner if your own house is teeming with leaks. I trust many of the individuals at the labs to work hard to ensure safety, but I’m not trustworthy of the institutions overall.

Open-weight Mythos in April would’ve been fine?

When Claude Mythos was announced, it was previewed as if it was a new class of cyber weapon, where if it ended up in the wrong hands it would’ve caused mass societal destabilization.

It seems like this was wrong.

By all measures, GLM-5.3 is the model that crosses that threshold of capability, and there’s little public evidence that much has changed, and we’re over a month out of the model weight release.

In fact, I would go further. If Claude Mythos was accidentally released as open-weight, it seems like the world would have been more or less fine. Yes, there would be a clear increase in cybersecurity incidents and it would be bad for society if the model leaked, but it would be a scenario that looks more like an acceleration than a step change in risk.

The leading proponents of this new wave of open-weight fear mongering have effectively been making a falsifiable prediction — that the current open-weight models are going to cause substantial, not seen before AI harms by crippling our cyber infrastructure.

Based on all the evidence I have, which I’ve unpacked above, they’re set up to be wrong. At least now, after so many years of debating open weight risks, we will start to get some real answers.

items.title: Developers are burned out, disengaged, and facing an AI-powered reset, a survey of 30,000 workers found
items.summary: Developers are embracing AI coding, but many feel exhausted, obsolete, and unable to trust it. Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images AI coding tools are speeding up work but leaving engineers anxious and depleted, Stack Overflow found. Nearly half the 30,000 developers surveyed said they are complacent, with burnout a major driver. "Keeping up with AI is virtually impossible," one software engineer told Business Insider. The people building the AI boom are running on empty. According to Stack Overflow's 2026 Developer Survey, released Tuesday, nearly half of 30,903 developers surveyed in 169 countries reported being complacent in their current jobs, while a third were unhappy, and just over 22% were happy. Among the complacent group, burnout or tech fatigue was the leading reason, cited by 21% of respondents. The findings come amid an environment where software engineers' jobs are changing at breakneck speed . AI coding has taken over a greater share of their daily work — reducing some developers to button-pushers and human meat proxies , contributing to an identity crisis among some engineers, and fueling "off-the-charts" anxiety among tech workers. The malaise comes alongside a major shift in how software gets made. Stack Overflow found that almost two-thirds of respondents use AI coding assistants or agents, while 62% use general-purpose AI chat tools. Among daily AI users, 31% said they use them for four hours or more. The findings echo what Annie Wright, a Bay Area psychotherapist and executive coach whose practice is dominated by tech workers, told Business Insider in August. Her clients had moved beyond ordinary burnout, she said, to questioning their identity and future as automation reshapes the work they have built their careers around. "Three years ago, people would walk in saying, 'I'm exhausted, burned out beyond belief,'" Wright said at the time. "Now they walk in saying, 'I'm exhausted. I'm burned out beyond belief. I don't know who I am if my work gets automated.'" A faster way to work — and more pressure to keep up Marc Backes, a senior software engineer at Directus, said AI has made his work less fulfilling. He used to enjoy working through a feature or tracing a technical problem to its source; now, he spends far more time asking AI agents to do it. "It's definitely less fulfilling," Backes told Business Insider. "I always enjoyed drafting out the best ways to implement a new feature and really think about it." The pressure is not coming directly from his manager, he said, but from an industry moving faster and treating writing — or even reading — code by hand as "the old way." "If I don't 'keep up,' I will be 'left behind,'" Backes said. "And keeping up with AI is virtually impossible." Not everyone feels diminished by the shift, though. Simon Willison, founder of the Datasette open-source project, said AI coding tools have made his work "a lot more fulfilling" by allowing him to take on projects that once might have required a small team. Willison said that being his own manager shields him from many of the pressures facing employed developers, though he still finds the pace of AI releases exhausting. "As an entrepreneur and product developer, I know that any space I operate in will be significantly more competitive now because the cost of developing software has dropped so much," he said. Still, Willison said he was optimistic about his career. "Using coding agents well is a deep skill," he said, one that requires both software-engineering knowledge and experience with the agents, "and I have both." Developers are using AI but want control Despite many using AI coding tools extensively, developers don't necessarily trust their output. The survey found that under 10% of respondents said they were prepared to trust AI for important decisions, while almost 80% said source attribution was important or very important when evaluating AI-generated code or technical answers. Prashanth Chandrasekar, Stack Overflow's CEO, said developers' skepticism was becoming a "critical safeguard" as agents took on more work. "Trust is not a given when it comes to developers," he said. "It is earned through transparency, source attribution, and rich technical context." Read the original article on Business Insider

The people building the AI boom are running on empty.

Among the complacent group, burnout or tech fatigue was the leading reason, cited by 21% of respondents.

The findings come amid an environment where software engineers' jobs are changing at breakneck speed. "Three years ago, people would walk in saying, 'I'm exhausted, burned out beyond belief,'" Wright said at the time. "Now they walk in saying, 'I'm exhausted. I'm burned out beyond belief. I don't know who I am if my work gets automated.'"

Marc Backes, a senior software engineer at Directus, said AI has made his work less fulfilling. He used to enjoy working through a feature or tracing a technical problem to its source; now, he spends far more time asking AI agents to do it.

"It's definitely less fulfilling," Backes told Business Insider. "I always enjoyed drafting out the best ways to implement a new feature and really think about it."

The pressure is not coming directly from his manager, he said, but from an industry moving faster and treating writing — or even reading — code by hand as "the old way."

"If I don't 'keep up,' I will be 'left behind,'" Backes said. "And keeping up with AI is virtually impossible."

Not everyone feels diminished by the shift, though.

items.title: AI Whistleblowers Say Researchers Are Checking AI Less Frequently
items.summary: It won’t be any surprise to people with human intelligence that Monday’s New York City Council hearing on the risks of AI was as theatrical as a Broadway show. What was more surprising was what the AI researchers testified about how AI research is evolving, and what that means for their job. For those who missed it, the city council heard testimony from three AI lab whistleblowers: Jacob Coxon , formerly of Anthropic and OpenAI ; Alex Turner , formerly of Google DeepMind ; and Daniel Kokotajlo , formerly of OpenAI. Afterwards, they heard from representatives of the AI labs. We’ll get to that lower down. One of the most interesting parts of the whistleblowers’ testimony related to the AI research process. Coxon and Kokotajlo each said that researchers at the labs have lately been letting AI drive the process of writing code and research. Researchers check AI’s work less frequently, they said. The labs might not agree with that exact characterization, although their representatives weren’t asked about it at the hearing. But the labs have been the first to say that AI has greatly accelerated the process of AI research. Anthropic even said in a report last month that, as of August, AI was leading more than a quarter of model research and development at the company.

items.title: Who owns ‘brain rot’?: inside the international legal drama over a beloved meme
items.summary: Copyright law in the US only applies to human-made creations, but AI characters like Tung Tung Tung Sahur are challenging that One of the most beloved characters in an absurdist genre of online video content has become the center of an international legal battle that could determine where human creativity ends and artificial intelligence begins. Tung Tung Tung Sahur, also known as Triple T, was created in 2025 by an Indonesian teen who goes by the username Noxa, using OpenAI’s image-generation tool. Based on a kentongan – a type of drum used to wake south-east Asian Muslims for their pre-dawn meal during Ramadan – the character is an anthropomorphized version of the instrument with a broad smile and a vacant stare. He sits under the umbrella of “Italian brain rot” internet videos.

items.title: The 14 most innovative influencer marketers of 2026
items.summary: Julian Wass; NFL; ALSAC; Alyssa Powell/BI Creators can hype up a brand or ruin its week in a single social media post. For marketers, figuring out how to tap into that influence is a balancing act. It requires experimentation, choosing the right influencer partners, handing over enough creative control, and reacting quickly when lightning strikes and your brand's name is suddenly all over the internet. Business Insider's 2026 list of the most innovative influencer marketers inside brands highlights the executives figuring out how to make their companies look good on social media. This year's 14 marketers were nominated by peers and other industry insiders who shared dozens of examples of how the marketers are working smartly with creators or making original content for social. Some, like PepsiCo's Charlie Crideford and Walmart's Sarah Henry, work with curated networks of influencers who make content or help advise on their social strategies. Others, like the National Football League's Ian Trombetta, work with large teams of in-house producers to make original content tailored to social feeds. Breaking through the noise means finding new audiences in different corners of the internet. Footwear brand Rothy's turned to Substack , for instance, to hire tastemaker writers who could help drive attention to its shoes. "We don't really care about follower count necessarily," Rothy's vice president Anna Doré said. "We really look for great partners and creators who have pull in their own circles, and that can be anyone these days." Our roster of innovative creator marketers faces challenges. Though the creator economy is booming, engagement is harder than ever to come by as social feeds become more saturated and algorithms surface content selectively to different users. "The creative bar is going up in order for us to drive that organic reach and engagement," the NFL's Trombetta said. "No one can predict exactly where the algorithms are going to go one day to the next." Here are Business Insider's 2026 most innovative influencer marketers, listed in alphabetical order by last name. Lindsay Burstein, Keurig Dr Pepper's senior director of integrated social and communications Lindsay Burstein Lindsay Burstein jumps into action when marketing opportunities show up unexpectedly, like when TikTok creator Romeo Bingham posted an impromptu Dr Pepper jingle that went viral and gathered over 100 million views. Burstein oversees a social team that works on creator partnerships, social listening, and digital community building at Keurig Dr Pepper, which has a portfolio of beverage brands like 7UP, Dr Pepper, and Snapple. "We're always looking for ways to do it faster and in a way that feels more real-time so that we're keeping up with the pace and the culture of the internet," Burstein said. In the case of the Bingham Dr Pepper jingle, the company reached out to the creator to license the song for a Dr Pepper commercial that aired during the College Football Playoff national championship. Other recent projects Burstein worked on included a 7UP LuluLime creator campaign tied to the US Open and a Snapple-sponsored comedy night with Pete Davidson and Colin Jost on their decommissioned Staten Island Ferry. Burstein works with celebrities and top influencers, as well as creators with smaller audiences who have posted positively about the company's brands. "We like to reward our fans," Burstein said. "An example could be letting them taste test a new flavor first. They're a big fan. Maybe we send them something that's going to be on the shelves in two weeks, like, 'Hey, we know you're a huge fan. Why don't you try this first?'" Charlie Crideford, PepsiCo's media strategy and deployment director for international beverages Charlie Crideford Charlie Crideford has turned Pepsi Max's creator efforts from an experiment into a pillar of its marketing since taking over the zero-sugar soda's UK work with creators in 2022. Working with the NewGen agency, Crideford grew Pepsi Pioneers, a program that uses creators to advise and shape campaigns for Pepsi, from 15 to 80 people across music, sports, food, and lifestyle. Over the past year, content created by Pioneers creators has more than tripled its reach, while the cost to reach those audiences has fallen by 61%. Under Crideford, Pioneers previously helped spark two highly impactful earned-media campaigns — Pepsi's Iconic Corner Shop and Cherry Ring Popper — and a Christmas TV spot. Crideford has more planned. She's aiming to make Pioneers a permanent part of PepsiCo's marketing approach. She's also extending the program to Ireland and the Nordics and building creator rosters for each market's culture. Anna Doré, Rothy's vice president of brand and communications Anna Doré Word of mouth is how Rothy's, the shoe brand best known for its comfortable flats, got on the map. Influencers are the next evolution of that, and Anna Doré knows it. Doré is turning to Substack to find the next generation of creators spreading the gospel about Rothy's shoes. "People follow these Substack writers because they are in the know," Doré said. "They are arbiters of taste." While Rothy's is still working with creators on Instagram and TikTok content, Substack has been a spot to experiment with its marketing. For example, as part of Rothy's 10-year anniversary marketing campaign, the brand partnered with five Substack creators to write essays about their own personal growth. Rothy's has seen an 18% year-over-year increase in mentions on the newsletter and blogging platform. Doré is also pushing for more in-real-life (IRL) marketing experiences with creators. Creators, especially Substackers, "want to take their communities out of the inbox and into the world," Doré said. Rothy's has been helping creators do just that, sponsoring niche events like a vintage pop-up or a pizza party. Events have real business impact, too. Rothy's worked with Substacker Erika Veurink on an in-store activation at one of the brand's New York locations, where Veurink hosted a vintage sale. The event brought in more than 200 people and increased store foot traffic by 75%, according to Rothy's. The brand also worked with Substacker and travel writer Denna Nazem after Doré spotted that the creator was organically talking about Rothy's shoes in her newsletter. It resulted in a travel-themed event promoting the launch of Rothy's at Nordstrom and a new collection of its shoes, boosting orders for its Cruiser collection and doubling product saves on the affiliate platform ShopMy. Substackers have "really rabid fans and followers who care deeply about what the writers are putting out there and want to connect in person," Doré said. Sarah Henry, Walmart's group director and head of content for influencer and commerce Sarah Henry Sarah Henry has expanded Walmart's creator marketing push, giving customers more ways to discover and shop at the retail giant. With oversight of content, influencer marketing, and social commerce, Henry integrated the hundreds of thousands of creators Walmart works with into its broader plans rather than treating them as a stand-alone marketing channel. Under Henry, the Walmart Creator program has grown from a small cohort in 2022 to a large network of brand advocates, and added new ways they can earn and work with brands. Walmart said dollar sales driven by the program have tripled in the past year. Henry has struck partnerships with affiliate platforms, including YouTube Shopping, ShopMy, and LTK. She has also pushed Walmart into creator-led entertainment content. This summer, she tapped creators like Nick DiGiovanni, Raven Elyse, and Eric Wang to develop original episodic series around dorm makeovers, cooking, and more to keep Walmart top of mind for back-to-school shoppers. Walmart said the series demonstrated that it can create shoppable content that drives purchases. Kemma Kefalas, Yahoo's senior director and head of Creative Lab Kemma Kefalas Kemma Kefalas rebuilt Yahoo's social strategy after joining in 2024, with dramatic results. Its TikTok and Instagram presence has soared, while her splashy creator-led campaigns have reintroduced a legacy brand to audiences. Kefalas' work with creators both raised awareness and contributed to tangible business results. Yahoo partnered with olive oil maker Graza ahead of the winter holidays to launch "Sssshhhhizzle" Keyboard Oil, a riff on the office archetype of the too-loud typer, continuing Yahoo's series of satirical "techcessories" that dramatize everyday digital frustrations. Boosted by LinkedIn influencers including Jade Walters and Brandon Smithwrick, the campaign earned nearly 3.5 million social views. For Planner, a new AI-driven feature in Yahoo Mail, Kefalas helped cast Cardi B for a campaign that tapped into what it called "FOMSI": Fear of Missing Something Important. Yahoo said the "Cardi B Busy" spot was its most-viewed, engaged-with, liked, and commented-on brand social post ever, and helped drive Yahoo Mail's app store rankings. The campaign delivered more than 10 million views and 600,000 likes across Yahoo's TikTok and Instagram accounts in its first two days. To launch a new Yahoo Weather app in July, Yahoo partnered with TV personality Kyle Cooke, the cofounder of Loverboy canned cocktails, as the "Weatherboy" to bring energy to the new app. And for April Fools' Day, Kemma's team introduced The Scrōll Stoppr, a $4.99 finger accessory that physically blocks the thumb from touching the screen. The product tapped into a universal pain point of mindless scrolling and promoted the idea of Yahoo as a brand that helps people get things done. Creators including Nicky Reardon, Gavin Fernand, and AJ Eckstein amplified the campaign, contributing to 4.5 million social views and 97 press stories, including an NBC News segment. Kiara Kempski, The Knot's vice president of global consumer marketing Kiara Kempski Engagement is a frequent buzzword in influencer marketing. But for The Knot, which connects millions of couples with wedding vendors, it means something more: a potential new creator to work with ahead of their nuptials. Kiara Kempski runs The Knot's lean but mighty influencer team, working with engaged influencers getting ready for their big day. In February, The Knot — which owns several wedding planning brands — launched a new ambassador program for couples called "The Knot Wedding Party." The Knot then takes that content from its ambassador program and repurposes it into paid media. The Knot's "Win a Honeymoon" campaign, which worked with creators to promote its sweepstakes, resulted in a 55% year-over-year increase in registry creations, according to the company. Kempski has focused The Knot's influencer strategy on nano and micro influencers — those with relatively small follower counts — who can tell everyday stories about the wedding-planning process. "Going with smaller creators gives us that breadth of different types of weddings and accessibility that's really important to couples, especially when we're trying to influence decision-making," Kempski said. Samantha Maltin, ALSAC's (St. Jude's fundraising organization) chief marketing and brand officer Julian Wass Samantha Maltin leads marketing and brand management for ALSAC, the fundraising organization behind St. Jude Children's Research Hospital. Previously a marketing exec at Sesame Street's Sesame Workshop, Maltin now focuses on growing St. Jude's brand awareness, overseeing a community management team that sets up creator and celebrity fundraising and marketing opportunities for St. Jude. "We vet very carefully any creator or influencer that we're going to work with," Maltin said. "We want to make sure that we share values, that they are as passionate about the mission as we are." Last year, Maltin's team worked with YouTuber Ryan Trahan to turn his "50 States in 50 Days" series into a fundraising campaign for St. Jude's, raising over $11.6 million for the research hospital. Stacy Martinet, Adobe's chief content and creative officer Adobe Longtime Adobe marketer Stacy Martinet led two of its most ambitious creator marketing stunts this past year, including major moments in Times Square and at Cannes Lions. For Firefly, Adobe's suite of AI tools, Martinet put the creator community that makes up a significant part of its customer base at the center of its "Just Imagine" campaign. Instead of using creators as spokespeople, Adobe created a documentary-style video series that featured the likes of Kinigra Deon, Valerie Zhang, and Pablo Rochat using Firefly in their own production work. Martinet then moved that idea to one of advertising's most iconic stages with a Times Square takeover this past spring. Twenty-three creators' Firefly-generated work lit up 38 screens across six city blocks, while self-serve stations let the public generate their own Firefly portraits that were published live onto 12-foot LED screens on-site. "Our goal was to say: We want people to know that Adobe Firefly is a place where you can move from ideation to creation into production very quickly," Martinet said. "And we wanted these creators to show how that works in their world." Adobe was also the first headline partner of Lions Creators, the creator-economy program of the Cannes Lions ad-industry blowout. More than 250 creators participated in the official Cannes creator programming. Adobe said the effort was its biggest Cannes investment to date. Martinet, who recently expanded her remit, will continue to make Adobe's case with creators at Adobe Max in November, its three-day creativity conference. Max will include initiatives such as the Creator Playground, a dedicated destination where influencers can create content on-site using Adobe's tools; a stand-alone Creator Track; and additional creator-economy programming. Christina Nguyen, Paramount Pictures' global creator marketing manager Christina Nguyen Christina Nguyen has helped usher creators from the sidelines of movie marketing into the center of the action. From sending creators onto sets, to pairing them with Hollywood stars, and building entire storylines around them, Nguyen's work has generated hundreds of millions of views and helped drive audiences to theaters. To build excitement for "Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning," Nguyen assembled creators from different niches — including Hero DW, Angelica Trae, Joe Mele, and Sam Hutchinson — for a social series in which basketball creator Lethal Shooter tried to solve an unfolding case. The story culminated at the film's red carpet premiere, where Lethal Shooter and Mele met Tom Cruise. For "Scream's" 30th anniversary, Nguyen and the team created a "Scream Kill Tour" T-shirt and sent it to actors who had played victims in the franchise. An initial limited-edition drop of 700 free tees was claimed almost instantly, prompting the company to release an updated version for sale on the Paramount Shop. Nguyen also demonstrates how being scrappy can pay off. Ahead of the cast filming a day of press interviews to promote the release of "By Any Means," Nguyen squeezed in 30 minutes for the YouTuber Adam W to quickly shoot some content with the film's stars. The resulting videos melded Adam W's comedic style with the movie's interrogation theme. They generated nearly 10 million views across Instagram and TikTok, per the creative agency Armed Mind, which works with Paramount Pictures. She's also breaking new ground in creator marketing with innovative partnerships. For the launch of "Running Man" last year, Nguyen and the team partnered with Strava to launch "The Running Man Challenge," encouraging top running creators and other users to complete 200 minutes of fitness activities within 30 days to unlock a special badge. More than 139,000 people participated, Strava said. "She truly approaches each title and opportunity as its own creative platform; a puzzle as opposed to an influencer-marketing formula that needs refreshing," said Michael Rudin, founder of Armed Mind. Patrick O'Keefe, E.l.f. Beauty's chief integrated marketing officer Patrick O'Keefe Patrick O'Keefe has helped make E.l.f. Cosmetics into a brand that creators want to actually create with, not simply promote. He does that by working with creators in ways that are native to their voices. This year, Emma Norton made a 2-minute cinematic adaptation of E.l.f.'s true crime-style mockumentary campaign tackling makeup clutter, "Vanity Vandals." It generated nearly 900,000 views and almost $90,000 in earned media value, a measure of the monetary worth of that exposure. A musical post she made for E.l.f.'s mock-horror campaign, Unglammy Valley, that poked fun at the difficulty of finding the right foundation shade, delivered similar results. Showing its sense of humor, E.l.f. tapped comedy creator Big Foot Bae, a pink bow-wearing Sasquatch, to amplify its Bigfoot-themed hair care campaign online and in person. E.l.f. said it was one of the company's most successful creator launches, generating more than 1,300 posts and reaching 166 million people. E.l.f. also knows when to jump into culture. When "Sailing with Phoenix," a creator who left his corporate life to sail with his cat, started gaining steam, E.l.f. dropped a care package to him in the middle of the ocean last year. The stunt went viral across social channels and traditional media . "E.l.f. is leaning into purpose, and what we saw was a guy living his dreams, and we wanted to be there to support him," O'Keefe said. Jason Ossenmacher, AAA Auto Club Enterprises' group manager of acquisition marketing Jason Ossenmacher Jason Ossenmacher has helped make creator marketing a top customer-acquisition channel at Auto Club Enterprises, the century-old member club within the American Automobile Association (AAA) federation, which has more than 17 million members. With consumers facing anxiety about rising costs, Ossenmacher identified that creator-content formats could help make AAA's products, in areas such as travel and home insurance, more personal and attainable. He's helped expand AAA's creator content across multiple channels, including Meta, TikTok, Pinterest, YouTube, Snap, and connected TV. Julian Wass; NFL; ALSAC; Alyssa Powell/BI

Creators can hype up a brand or ruin its week in a single social media post.

For marketers, figuring out how to tap into that influence is a balancing act. It requires experimentation, choosing the right influencer partners, handing over enough creative control, and reacting quickly when lightning strikes and your brand's name is suddenly all over the internet.

Business Insider's 2026 list of the most innovative influencer marketers inside brands highlights the executives figuring out how to make their companies look good on social media. This year's 14 marketers were nominated by peers and other industry insiders who shared dozens of examples of how the marketers are working smartly with creators or making original content for social.

Some, like PepsiCo's Charlie Crideford and Walmart's Sarah Henry, work with curated networks of influencers who make content or help advise on their social strategies. Others, like the National Football League's Ian Trombetta, work with large teams of in-house producers to make original content tailored to social feeds.

Breaking through the noise means finding new audiences in different corners of the internet. Footwear brand Rothy's turned to Substack, for instance, to hire tastemaker writers who could help drive attention to its shoes.

"We don't really care about follower count necessarily," Rothy's vice president Anna Doré said. "We really look for great partners and creators who have pull in their own circles, and that can be anyone these days."

Our roster of innovative creator marketers faces challenges. Though the creator economy is booming, engagement is harder than ever to come by as social feeds become more saturated and algorithms surface content selectively to different users.

"The creative bar is going up in order for us to drive that organic reach and engagement," the NFL's Trombetta said. "No one can predict exactly where the algorithms are going to go one day to the next."

Here are Business Insider's 2026 most innovative influencer marketers, listed in alphabetical order by last name.

Lindsay Burstein, Keurig Dr Pepper's senior director of integrated social and communications

Lindsay Burstein

Lindsay Burstein jumps into action when marketing opportunities show up unexpectedly, like when TikTok creator Romeo Bingham posted an impromptu Dr Pepper jingle that went viral and gathered over 100 million views.

Burstein oversees a social team that works on creator partnerships, social listening, and digital community building at Keurig Dr Pepper, which has a portfolio of beverage brands like 7UP, Dr Pepper, and Snapple.

"We're always looking for ways to do it faster and in a way that feels more real-time so that we're keeping up with the pace and the culture of the internet," Burstein said.

In the case of the Bingham Dr Pepper jingle, the company reached out to the creator to license the song for a Dr Pepper commercial that aired during the College Football Playoff national championship.

Other recent projects Burstein worked on included a 7UP LuluLime creator campaign tied to the US Open and a Snapple-sponsored comedy night with Pete Davidson and Colin Jost on their decommissioned Staten Island Ferry.

Burstein works with celebrities and top influencers, as well as creators with smaller audiences who have posted positively about the company's brands.

"We like to reward our fans," Burstein said. "An example could be letting them taste test a new flavor first. They're a big fan. Maybe we send them something that's going to be on the shelves in two weeks, like, 'Hey, we know you're a huge fan. Why don't you try this first?'"

Charlie Crideford, PepsiCo's media strategy and deployment director for international beverages

Charlie Crideford

Charlie Crideford has turned Pepsi Max's creator efforts from an experiment into a pillar of its marketing since taking over the zero-sugar soda's UK work with creators in 2022.

Working with the NewGen agency, Crideford grew Pepsi Pioneers, a program that uses creators to advise and shape campaigns for Pepsi, from 15 to 80 people across music, sports, food, and lifestyle.

Over the past year, content created by Pioneers creators has more than tripled its reach, while the cost to reach those audiences has fallen by 61%. Under Crideford, Pioneers previously helped spark two highly impactful earned-media campaigns — Pepsi's Iconic Corner Shop and Cherry Ring Popper — and a Christmas TV spot.

Crideford has more planned. She's aiming to make Pioneers a permanent part of PepsiCo's marketing approach. She's also extending the program to Ireland and the Nordics and building creator rosters for each market's culture.

Anna Doré, Rothy's vice president of brand and communications

Anna Doré

Word of mouth is how Rothy's, the shoe brand best known for its comfortable flats, got on the map. Influencers are the next evolution of that, and Anna Doré knows it.

Doré is turning to Substack to find the next generation of creators spreading the gospel about Rothy's shoes.

"People follow these Substack writers because they are in the know," Doré said. "They are arbiters of taste."

While Rothy's is still working with creators on Instagram and TikTok content, Substack has been a spot to experiment with its marketing. For example, as part of Rothy's 10-year anniversary marketing campaign, the brand partnered with five Substack creators to write essays about their own personal growth. Rothy's has seen an 18% year-over-year increase in mentions on the newsletter and blogging platform.

Doré is also pushing for more in-real-life (IRL) marketing experiences with creators. Creators, especially Substackers, "want to take their communities out of the inbox and into the world," Doré said. Rothy's has been helping creators do just that, sponsoring niche events like a vintage pop-up or a pizza party.

Events have real business impact, too. Rothy's worked with Substacker Erika Veurink on an in-store activation at one of the brand's New York locations, where Veurink hosted a vintage sale. The event brought in more than 200 people and increased store foot traffic by 75%, according to Rothy's. The brand also worked with Substacker and travel writer Denna Nazem after Doré spotted that the creator was organically talking about Rothy's shoes in her newsletter. It resulted in a travel-themed event promoting the launch of Rothy's at Nordstrom and a new collection of its shoes, boosting orders for its Cruiser collection and doubling product saves on the affiliate platform ShopMy.

Substackers have "really rabid fans and followers who care deeply about what the writers are putting out there and want to connect in person," Doré said.

Sarah Henry

Sarah Henry has expanded Walmart's creator marketing push, giving customers more ways to discover and shop at the retail giant.

With oversight of content, influencer marketing, and social commerce, Henry integrated the hundreds of thousands of creators Walmart works with into its broader plans rather than treating them as a stand-alone marketing channel.

Under Henry, the Walmart Creator program has grown from a small cohort in 2022 to a large network of brand advocates, and added new ways they can earn and work with brands. Walmart said dollar sales driven by the program have tripled in the past year.

Henry has struck partnerships with affiliate platforms, including YouTube Shopping, ShopMy, and LTK.

She has also pushed Walmart into creator-led entertainment content. This summer, she tapped creators like Nick DiGiovanni, Raven Elyse, and Eric Wang to develop original episodic series around dorm makeovers, cooking, and more to keep Walmart top of mind for back-to-school shoppers. Walmart said the series demonstrated that it can create shoppable content that drives purchases.

Kemma Kefalas

Kemma Kefalas rebuilt Yahoo's social strategy after joining in 2024, with dramatic results. Its TikTok and Instagram presence has soared, while her splashy creator-led campaigns have reintroduced a legacy brand to audiences.

Kefalas' work with creators both raised awareness and contributed to tangible business results.

Yahoo partnered with olive oil maker Graza ahead of the winter holidays to launch "Sssshhhhizzle" Keyboard Oil, a riff on the office archetype of the too-loud typer, continuing Yahoo's series of satirical "techcessories" that dramatize everyday digital frustrations. Boosted by LinkedIn influencers including Jade Walters and Brandon Smithwrick, the campaign earned nearly 3.5 million social views.

For Planner, a new AI-driven feature in Yahoo Mail, Kefalas helped cast Cardi B for a campaign that tapped into what it called "FOMSI": Fear of Missing Something Important. Yahoo said the "Cardi B Busy" spot was its most-viewed, engaged-with, liked, and commented-on brand social post ever, and helped drive Yahoo Mail's app store rankings. The campaign delivered more than 10 million views and 600,000 likes across Yahoo's TikTok and Instagram accounts in its first two days.

Twenty-three creators' Firefly-generated work lit up 38 screens across six city blocks, while self-serve stations let the public generate their own Firefly portraits that were published live onto 12-foot LED screens on-site.

"Our goal was to say: We want people to know that Adobe Firefly is a place where you can move from ideation to creation into production very quickly," Martinet said. "And we wanted these creators to show how that works in their world."

Adobe was also the first headline partner of Lions Creators, the creator-economy program of the Cannes Lions ad-industry blowout. More than 250 creators participated in the official Cannes creator programming. Adobe said the effort was its biggest Cannes investment to date.

Martinet, who recently expanded her remit, will continue to make Adobe's case with creators at Adobe Max in November, its three-day creativity conference. Max will include initiatives such as the Creator Playground, a dedicated destination where influencers can create content on-site using Adobe's tools; a stand-alone Creator Track; and additional creator-economy programming.

Christina Nguyen has helped usher creators from the sidelines of movie marketing into the center of the action.

items.title: What Claude Code Keeps of Your Skills After Compaction
items.summary: A 5,000-token snapshot, a 25,000-token shared budget, and a skill index that never comes back. The mechanics, the failure modes, and the patterns that hold up in long sessions. Three hours into a session, Claude Code is midway through a database migration. Early on you invoked a db-migration-review skill that requires every schema change to ship with a rollback script. For the first forty minutes, every change came with one. Then auto-compaction ran. The next migration arrives without a rollback, and nothing in the terminal says why. The skill wasn’t deleted. Part of it was kept, part was cut, and the part that was kept no longer has the weight it had when it was the most recent instruction in the conversation. If you build skills for other people to use, you need to know exactly which part is which. This article covers documented behaviour as of Claude Code’s current docs, with community-reported behaviour labelled as such. The numbers below are implementation details and have changed before, so treat them as values to re-check on upgrades, not constants. Skills in context after compaction in Claude Code How a skill sits in context A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md file and optional supporting files. At session start, Claude Code loads a listing : one line per available skill, built from the description and when_to_use frontmatter. Each combined entry is truncated at 1,536 characters. Skills marked disable-model-invocation: true stay out of the listing entirely until someone types /name. When a skill is invoked, by Claude through the Skill tool or by you with /name, Claude Code renders SKILL.md and appends it to the conversation as a single message . Several properties follow from that: The file is read once. Claude Code does not re-read SKILL.md on later turns. Edits you make on disk mid-session have no effect until the skill is invoked again. Re-invoking is deduplicated by content. If the rendered output is identical to what is already in context, Claude Code adds a short “already loaded” note. If arguments or dynamic output changed, the full body is appended again. !command blocks are frozen at render time. Lines like !`git diff HEAD` run once before the content reaches the model, and their output becomes plain text inside the message. That text doesn't refresh. allowed-tools is scoped to one turn. The permission grant applies during the turn that invoked the skill and clears when you send your next message. The instructions stay; the pre-approvals don't. The skill’s text lives in conversation history. Compaction rewrites conversation history. Everything that follows comes from that. What compaction does When context approaches its limit, or when you run /compact, Claude Code replaces the conversation with a structured summary. According to the context window documentation , the summary keeps your requests and intent, key technical concepts, files examined or modified with important snippets, errors and their fixes, pending tasks, and current work. Full tool outputs and intermediate reasoning are discarded. Content that lives outside the message history is then reloaded: System prompt and output style still apply. Project-root CLAUDE.md, unscoped rules and auto memory are re-injected from disk. A fresh git status snapshot is taken. A plan written in plan mode is re-injected from disk. Up to five recently read or edited files are re-read, most recently modified first. Any file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path reference only. SessionStart hooks that match the compact source run, and their output is added. Content that lived inside message history is handled case by case: Path-scoped rules (paths: frontmatter) and nested CLAUDE.md files are summarised away. They reload only when Claude reads a matching file again. Context added earlier by hooks is summarised with everything else. Invoked skills get special treatment, described next. The skill listing is not re-injected. The skill re-attachment rule The skills documentation states the rule precisely. After the summary, Claude Code re-attaches the most recent invocation of each skill , keeping the first 5,000 tokens of each. All re-attached skills share a combined budget of 25,000 tokens , filled starting from the most recently invoked skill. Older skills can be dropped entirely. Three details matter in practice. Truncation keeps the head. Whatever sits beyond roughly the 5,000th token of the rendered skill is gone. A skill that puts its workflow first and its constraints in a closing “Important rules” section loses the constraints first. “Under 500 lines” is not the same as “under 5,000 tokens.” The docs recommend keeping SKILL.md under 500 lines. Markdown prose runs about 4 characters per token, so a 500-line skill at an average of 60 characters per line is around 30,000 characters, or about 7,500 tokens. That fits the authoring guideline and still exceeds the compaction cap by half. Rendered !command output counts too: a skill that injects a large git diff can blow its own budget before you write a line of instructions. Eviction is by recency, not importance. If a session invoked a 4,000-token governance skill early and then five 5,000-token productivity skills later, the governance skill is the one that falls off. The budget has no concept of priority. Five ways a skill degrades after compaction Truncation. The tail of a long skill disappears, cutting at the token boundary rather than a section boundary. Eviction. Older skills disappear completely once the 25,000-token budget is spent. Routing blindness. Because the listing isn’t re-injected, Claude loses the trigger descriptions for skills that were never invoked. In sessions with many installed skills, requests that should route to a skill get handled with raw tools instead. This is tracked in anthropics/claude-code#82017 , which reports the problem with around 85 registered skills. Stale dynamic context. Re-attached content carries the original !command output. A skill that injected the branch state or a config snapshot now carries data from hours ago, with nothing marking it as old. Loss of weight. This one is community-reported rather than documented. In anthropics/claude-code#95745 , a user describes CLAUDE.md rules present in context after /compact but no longer followed, while an imperative SessionStart hook in the same context was honoured. The likely explanation is structural: in a fresh session, instructions frame the task; after compaction, the summary becomes the frame and re-injected instructions arrive as attachments behind it. Being in context is not the same as being followed. The official guidance for the first two is short: if Claude stops following a skill partway through a session, invoke it again. Why printing the skill from a hook is the wrong fix The obvious workaround is a SessionStart hook with the compact matcher that runs cat on SKILL.md.
